---
title: "CodeBook Lab"
---

CodeBook Studio and CodeBook Lab are two open-source tools for annotating text with large language models (LLMs) and checking the results against human coders. Both read the same codebook, so the instructions human coders follow are the instructions the model receives.

- **CodeBook Studio** is a web app for writing a codebook and annotating texts by hand. You upload a CSV, define the questions coders answer (checkboxes, dropdowns, Likert scales, free text and text highlights), annotate in the browser, and export the codebook and your labels. Use it at [codebook.streamlit.app](https://codebook.streamlit.app/) or run it on your own machine.
- **CodeBook Lab** is a Python package that annotates the same texts with local LLMs through [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) and scores the model's labels against the human ones. It records accuracy and agreement for every field, alongside runtime, energy use and estimated emissions, so you can compare models, prompts and settings on the same task.

## How Studio And Lab Fit Together

A typical project moves through these steps:

1. **Write the codebook in Studio.** Group questions into sections, add instructions and worked examples, and make questions conditional on earlier answers where needed.
2. **Annotate a sample by hand.** One coder can annotate in Studio directly. With several coders, Lab measures their agreement and builds a consensus label file, and you resolve the remaining disagreements in Studio (see [Human Reliability](human-reliability.qmd)).
3. **Export two files**: `codebook.json` and `ground-truth.csv`. Together they form a Lab [task](tasks.qmd).
4. **Run experiments in Lab.** Each run sends every text to a model, one question at a time, and saves the model's answers.
5. **Compare the results.** Lab scores each run against the human labels and appends the scores to two tidy tables you can analyse in Python or R.

## What Lab Does In A Run

For each experiment, Lab:

1. Loads the task folder: `codebook.json` and `ground-truth.csv`.
2. Removes the human label columns, so the model never sees the answers it is scored against.
3. Builds a prompt for each question from the codebook (section instruction, question, guidance, allowed answers and, optionally, worked examples) and sends it to the model with the text. See [What the model sees](experiments.qmd#what-the-model-sees).
4. Checks each answer against the codebook. Invalid answers are retried, and recorded as blank if they still fail.
5. Saves the model's labels and the run settings in a folder of its own.
6. Scores the labels against the human ones with metrics suited to each question type, and logs runtime, characters sent and received, energy use and estimated emissions.

Lab supports the same five question types as Studio: checkbox, dropdown, Likert, textbox and span. Conditional questions are skipped when they don't apply, both when prompting and when scoring. Textbox and span questions are only run when you switch them on, because their metrics need extra dependencies or source texts.

## Where To Start

- **To try the whole workflow quickly**, follow [Installation](install.qmd), then run the bundled `policy-sentiment` task in [Examples](examples.qmd).
- **If you already have Studio exports**, check them against [Tasks](tasks.qmd) and [Annotation Types](annotation-types.qmd), then run them as in [Experiments](experiments.qmd).
- **If you are starting a new annotation project**, begin with the [CodeBook Studio](studio.qmd) guide.
